idiom_name: hand-declared `Copy()`/`Clone()` on the base type; `MemberwiseClone()` for the field copy, records + `with` for statically typed copies
implementation_notes: To copy through a base class or interface reference in C# you must declare the copy operation yourself and implement it in every concrete type; the language supplies only helpers. `Object.MemberwiseClone()` is the field-by-field copier (protected, shallow, no constructor runs), a record's compiler-synthesised copy constructor plus the `with` expression (C# 9) gives non-destructive copies when the static type is known, and `ICloneable` is explicitly vetoed by Microsoft for public APIs because `Clone()` does not say whether the copy is shallow or deep. So: a typed `DeepCopy()`/`Copy()` on the base type (interface methods cannot be overridden, so the abstract/virtual form lives on a base class or is implemented per type), and `with` for the common statically typed case. Note that the name `Clone` is reserved inside records (CS8859), so a record cannot declare one and has to expose the operation under another name (`Copy`, `DeepClone`).
pitfalls: `MemberwiseClone()` is shallow: every reference field (List<T>, arrays, nested objects) is shared with the original, so mutating the copy's collection is visible in the original - deep-copy each mutable field in the copy constructor.

`ICloneable.Clone()` returns `object` and leaves deep-versus-shallow unspecified, so callers cast on faith; Microsoft recommends not implementing it in public APIs - prefer a typed `Copy()`/`DeepCopy()`.

Inside a record the compiler reserves the name `Clone` (CS8859): a member named `Clone` fails to compile, and records must also be in a record hierarchy (records may inherit only from records) for the copy constructor chain to work.
